profile.feeling: Green pods from Greek, Turkish, Arab and Indian kitchens – loved or disliked for their slime.

senses.def: okra (Abelmoschus esculentus and its green pods)

examples.text: Okra wird beim Kochen etwas schleimig.
examples.tr: Okra gets a little slimy when cooked.

examples.text: In Griechenland heißen Okras Bamies und werden mit Tomaten geschmort.
examples.tr: In Greece okra is called bamies and is stewed with tomatoes.

examples.text: Im türkischen Supermarkt gibt es frische Okras.
examples.tr: There is fresh okra at the Turkish supermarket.

synonyms.nuance: the Arabic/Turkish name, used in Turkish and Arabic shops
botanical name (“vegetable marshmallow”)

etymology.text: From an unknown West African language, perhaps via English okra.

funFacts: Greek μπάμιες, Turkish bamya, Arabic بَامِيَة (bāmiya) and Hebrew בַּמְיָה (bamya) are all the same word – German Bamia comes from it too.
pitfalls: Plural Okras; one pod is eine Okra or eine Okraschote.
subtleties: The slime (mucilage) is wanted in some dishes as a thickener and avoided in others by frying the pods or adding acid.

profile.feeling: An old European field crop: big green beans, peasant food and modern plant protein.

examples.text: Die Ackerbohne ist eine sehr alte Kulturpflanze.
examples.tr: The broad bean is a very old crop.

examples.text: Junge Ackerbohnen schmecken frisch und leicht süß.
examples.tr: Young broad beans taste fresh and slightly sweet.

examples.text: Im Supermarkt heißen Ackerbohnen meistens „dicke Bohnen“.
examples.tr: In the supermarket broad beans are usually called “dicke Bohnen”.

synonyms.nuance: the usual name in cooking and shops, especially in western Germany
name in Austria and southern Germany, where the bean was mostly fodder
another descriptive name

etymology.text: Acker (“field”, from Old High German ackar) + Bohne (“bean”, from Old High German bōna, cognate with English bean).

funFacts: Arabic فُول (fūl), as in the Egyptian dish fūl medames, and Hebrew פּוֹל (pol) name this bean; Greek says κουκιά, Turkish bakla.
pitfalls: Some people with an inherited enzyme deficiency (G6PD) must not eat them: favism.
Do not confuse with grüne Bohnen (green beans, Bohne in veg.1).
subtleties: Before the Phaseolus beans arrived from America, this was the bean of Europe.

profile.feeling: Wrinkled green gourd of Asian cooking – bitter on purpose.

examples.text: Die Bittermelone ist grün und hat eine warzige Schale.
examples.tr: The bitter melon is green and has a warty skin.

examples.text: Bittermelone ist so bitter, dass man sie vor dem Kochen oft salzt.
examples.tr: Bitter melon is so bitter that people often salt it before cooking.

examples.text: In Okinawa brät man Bittermelone mit Tofu und Ei.
examples.tr: In Okinawa bitter melon is stir-fried with tofu and egg.

synonyms.nuance: equally common name (“bitter cucumber”)
after the Okinawan name goya

etymology.text: From bitter + Melone; Melone is from Italian melone and Middle French melon, from Late Latin mēlō, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn).

funFacts: Chinese 苦瓜 (kǔguā) also means literally “bitter melon”.
pitfalls: It is not a sweet melon: it is cooked as a vegetable.
subtleties: The bitterness is valued in Asian cooking and traditional medicine rather than hidden.

profile.feeling: Gourds turned into bottles, bowls and drums; a mild vegetable when young.

examples.text: Aus getrockneten Flaschenkürbissen macht man Gefäße und Instrumente.
examples.tr: Containers and instruments are made from dried bottle gourds.

examples.text: Junge Flaschenkürbisse kann man wie Zucchini kochen.
examples.tr: Young bottle gourds can be cooked like courgettes.

examples.text: In Indien heißt der Flaschenkürbis Lauki.
examples.tr: In India the bottle gourd is called lauki.

collocations.tr: a vessel made from a bottle gourd

synonyms.nuance: especially the dried fruit used as a container or instrument

etymology.text: From Flasche (“bottle”) + -n- + Kürbis (“gourd, pumpkin”).

funFacts: It is one of the oldest cultivated plants, used as a container long before pottery; Chinese calls it 葫芦 (húlu).
pitfalls: Masculine like Kürbis: der Flaschenkürbis, des Flaschenkürbisses, plural die Flaschenkürbisse.
subtleties: Only young, tender fruits are eaten; ripe ones become hard and woody.

profile.feeling: Mediterranean delicacy: leaf by leaf, dipped in sauce, down to the tender heart.

senses.def: artichoke (the edible flower bud of Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus)

examples.text: Bei der Artischocke isst man den unteren Teil der Blätter und den Boden.
examples.tr: With an artichoke you eat the lower part of the leaves and the base.

examples.text: Artischockenherzen aus dem Glas passen gut auf die Pizza.
examples.tr: Artichoke hearts from a jar go well on pizza.

examples.text: Die Artischocke ist eigentlich eine Blütenknospe.
examples.tr: The artichoke is actually a flower bud.

etymology.text: From Northern Italian articiocco, from Provençal archichaut, from Old Spanish alcarchofa, from Andalusian Arabic الْخَرْشُوف (al-ḵaršūf), from Arabic الْخُرْشُوف (al-ḵuršūf).

funFacts: The word goes back to Arabic (al-)ḵuršūf; Hebrew has the related חֻרְשָׁף (ḥuršaf), Greek αγκινάρα, Turkish enginar.
pitfalls: Plural Artischocken. The hairy “choke” inside (das Heu) is not eaten.
subtleties: The bitter Italian liqueur Cynar is made with artichoke and named after its Latin name Cynara.

compound.none: a simple word (from Italian cavoli rape)

profile.feeling: A typically German vegetable: crunchy, mild, eaten raw as a snack or in a light sauce.

examples.text: Kohlrabi kann man roh als Snack essen.
examples.tr: You can eat kohlrabi raw as a snack.

examples.text: Beim Kohlrabi wächst die Knolle über der Erde.
examples.tr: With kohlrabi the bulb grows above the ground.

examples.text: Heute koche ich Kohlrabi in einer hellen Soße.
examples.tr: Today I am cooking kohlrabi in a white sauce.

synonyms.nuance: Austrian name for kohlrabi (elsewhere Kohlrübe means rutabaga)

funFacts: English kohlrabi and Russian кольраби were borrowed from German.
pitfalls: Masculine: der Kohlrabi, plural die Kohlrabis.
subtleties: The “bulb” is a thickened stem, not a root.

plurals.none: a mass noun: used without a plural

profile.feeling: Little green rosettes – the childhood vegetable many people hated, now milder and back in fashion.

examples.text: Viele Kinder mögen keinen Rosenkohl.

examples.tr: Brussels sprouts taste milder after the first frost.

examples.text: In Österreich heißt Rosenkohl Kohlsprossen.
examples.tr: In Austria Brussels sprouts are called Kohlsprossen.

synonyms.nuance: the Austrian word (die Kohlsprossen, plural)

etymology.text: Rose + -n- + Kohl. Named after the rose-shaped part that is eaten.

funFacts: English and French name it after Brussels (Brussels sprouts, choux de Bruxelles); German names it after its rose-like shape.
pitfalls: No plural: Rosenkohl is uncountable; one sprout is ein Röschen or ein Rosenkohlröschen.
subtleties: Newer varieties are less bitter than the ones many adults remember from childhood.

profile.feeling: A pale-green, pear-shaped gourd from Central America and the Caribbean; mild and crunchy.

examples.text: In der Karibik nennt man die Chayote auch Christophine.

examples.text: Chayoten kann man roh in den Salat reiben oder kochen.
examples.tr: Chayotes can be grated raw into salad or cooked.

synonyms.nuance: the Caribbean name, also used in German

funFacts: The fruit contains a single large, flat seed.
pitfalls: Feminine: die Chayote, plural die Chayoten; pronounced tscha-JO-te.
subtleties: It belongs to the gourd family, like Kürbis and Gurke.

profile.feeling: A huge pale gourd from Chinese cooking, used in clear soups.

examples.tr: A whole winter melon keeps for months.

examples.text: In China kocht man Suppe mit Wachskürbis.
examples.tr: In China soup is cooked with winter melon.

synonyms.nuance: translated from the English name

funFacts: Chinese 冬瓜 (dōngguā) means “winter melon” – it keeps until winter.
pitfalls: Masculine like Kürbis: der Wachskürbis, des Wachskürbisses, plural die Wachskürbisse.

profile.feeling: From vegetable to bath sponge: a gourd that turns into a natural scrubber.

examples.text: Aus der getrockneten Schwammgurke macht man einen Luffaschwamm.
examples.tr: A loofah sponge is made from the dried sponge gourd.

examples.text: Junge Schwammgurken isst man in Asien als Gemüse.
examples.tr: In Asia young sponge gourds are eaten as a vegetable.

examples.text: Die Schwammgurke wächst an langen Ranken.
examples.tr: The sponge gourd grows on long tendrils.

synonyms.nuance: the botanical and trade name, best known from bath sponges

etymology.text: From Schwamm (“sponge”) + Gurke (“cucumber”); Gurke is borrowed from Old Polish ogórek, from Byzantine Greek ἀγγούριον.

funFacts: Luffa comes from Arabic لُوفَة (lūfa), the same word as English loofah.
pitfalls: Feminine because of Gurke: die Schwammgurke, plural die Schwammgurken.
subtleties: Only young fruits are edible; ripe ones dry into a fibrous net – the sponge.

profile.feeling: Northern German winter tradition – kale tours, sausage and schnapps – and a modern superfood.

senses.def: kale stew, a winter dish of northern Germany

examples.text: Grünkohl schmeckt nach dem ersten Frost am besten.
examples.tr: Kale tastes best after the first frost.

examples.text: Im Winter machen wir mit Freunden eine Kohlfahrt und essen danach Grünkohl mit Pinkel.
examples.tr: In winter we go on a kale tour with friends and then eat kale with Pinkel sausage.

examples.text: Heute gibt es bei uns Grünkohl.
examples.tr: Today we are having kale stew.

examples.text: Grünkohl ist inzwischen auch als Superfood beliebt.
examples.tr: Kale has now also become popular as a superfood.

synonyms.nuance: regional name in parts of northern Germany
less common name, after the feathery leaves
joking name: the tall plant as the “palm tree of northern Germany”

funFacts: On a Kohlfahrt groups walk through the winter countryside with a handcart of drinks, then eat kale; the best eater may be crowned Kohlkönig.
pitfalls: The plural Grünkohle is rare; normally uncountable.

compound.none: two words (from Cantonese), not a German compound

senses.def: bok choy, pak choi (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis)

examples.text: Pak Choi brät man kurz im Wok mit Knoblauch und Ingwer.

examples.text: Den Pak Choi längs halbieren und gut waschen.

synonyms.nuance: hyphenated spelling of the same word
alternative spelling

funFacts: In Mandarin 白菜 (báicài) usually means napa cabbage (Chinakohl) – the same characters, a different vegetable.

examples.tr: I cut the napa cabbage into fine strips for the salad.

synonyms.nuance: older name, “Peking cabbage”

examples.tr: Smoked jalapeños are called chipotle.

funFacts: The city name Xalapa comes from Nahuatl, from xalli (“sand”) and atl (“water”).
pitfalls: Masculine (der Jalapeño, Duden); plural die Jalapeños. The ñ is often written n in shops (Jalapeno).

used in the west and south-west
rarer regional name

pitfalls: The plural Rotkohle is rare; say zwei Köpfe Rotkohl.

senses.def: runner bean, scarlet runner bean (Phaseolus coccineus)

examples.text: Die Feuerbohne hat leuchtend rote Blüten.
examples.tr: The runner bean has bright red flowers.

examples.text: In der Steiermark isst man Käferbohnen, das sind Feuerbohnen.

profile.feeling: Big flat cabbage leaves: soul food of the American South, little known in Germany.

examples.text: Blattkohl bildet keinen Kopf, sondern nur große Blätter.

examples.text: In den Südstaaten der USA isst man Blattkohl als Collard Greens.

examples.text: Blattkohl muss länger kochen als Spinat.

examples.text: Sojasprossen sind meistens eigentlich Mungbohnensprossen.

profile.feeling: Autumn markets and creamy soups: a pear-shaped, sweet and nutty squash.

examples.text: Den Butternusskürbis muss man vor dem Kochen schälen.

profile.feeling: Flat, sweet, crunchy pods – Asian stir-fries and quick side dishes.

examples.text: Zuckerschoten isst man mit der Schote.
examples.tr: Snow peas are eaten with the pod.

examples.text: Zuckerschoten brate ich nur kurz, damit sie knackig bleiben.
examples.tr: I fry snow peas only briefly so that they stay crunchy.

examples.text: In der Schweiz heißen Zuckerschoten Kefen.

the Swiss word (die Kefe, plural Kefen)
often used for the same pods, but also for the plump sugar snap pea

etymology.text: Zucker (“sugar”) + Schote (“pod”).

funFacts: Chinese calls them 荷兰豆 (hélándòu), “Dutch beans”; French mangetout means “eat-all”.
pitfalls: Pull off the string along the edge before cooking.
